title: BluePeak AI - quickstart + first production launch checklist demo
summary: Redwood demoed the in-Console onboarding + “first production launch” checklist prototype and walked BluePeak AI through the updated Hosted API quickstart (streaming chat, retries/timeouts, and observability basics). BluePeak’s main concerns were around quota/rate-limit surprises, cost controls (hard budget caps vs alerts), and how quickly usage dashboards reflect spend. Redwood clarified quota vs rate limits, pointed to budget alert options and recommended client-side backoff patterns, and proposed next steps: enable a sandbox tenant for BluePeak, share the checklist doc links and a production readiness quickstart, and schedule a follow-up focused on quotas/budgets and rollout/fallback policies.
topics: Checklist prototype in Redwood Console (step states, deep links, admin/support overrides)
Updated quickstart and “production-safe defaults” (timeouts, retries, streaming reconnect guidance)
Quotas, rate limits (429), and cost controls (budgets/alerts vs hard caps)
Usage dashboard latency / data freshness expectations
Model pinning and fallback policy basics for first production traffic
Telemetry/eventing: what’s tracked, PII avoidance, retention
next_steps: Redwood to send BluePeak the production readiness quickstart + streaming chat example links and the checklist step list (draft) after the call.
Redwood to provision a sandbox Hosted API tenant with the checklist feature flag enabled for BluePeak to try.
BluePeak to share their expected traffic ramp (QPS, token mix) and desired monthly spend guardrails for a quota/budget configuration recommendation.
Schedule a 30-minute follow-up (SE-led) to deep dive on quota/budget alerting + recommended backoff and the “first production launch” steps.
action_items: Ben Carter: Email recap with links to quickstart, streaming example, and checklist doc by 2025-03-05.
Sabrina James: Provide recommended retry/backoff + timeout defaults for TS/Python for BluePeak’s streaming workload by 2025-03-07.
Wei Chen: Confirm current behavior/ETA for in-Console budgets vs alerts (and any hard-limit options) and report back by 2025-03-07.
Avery Park: Send BluePeak’s expected ramp + max spend threshold and whether they want “hard stop” behavior or alert-only by 2025-03-07.
transcript:
Meeting: BluePeak AI - quickstart + first production launch checklist demo
Recorded: 2025-03-04 10:02 AM PT
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Ben Carter (AE), Sabrina James (Solutions/SE), Wei Chen (DevEx/Docs)
- BluePeak AI: Avery Park (CTO), Ravi Singh (Staff Eng), Jordan Ellis (Product)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Redwood walked through new in-product checklist + updated quickstart.
- BluePeak asked about quotas, budgets, and cost overruns.
- Next steps: sandbox access + follow-up on quota/budget settings.


[00:00] Ben Carter: Cool, alright. I think we’re all here. Avery, Ravi, Jordan—good to see you again. Today we wanted to show you the updated quickstart and this new “first production launch” checklist we’re rolling into the Console. It’s meant to make that jump from first call to actual prod traffic less… hand-wavy.

[00:17] Avery Park: Yeah, sounds good. We’re trying to avoid the situation where we get a demo working and then the first real traffic hits and everything’s on fire.

[00:24] Ben Carter: Exactly. Sabrina’s gonna drive most of the demo. Wei’s here because the quickstart and docs are getting updated in parallel.

[00:32] Sabrina James: Hey everyone. I’m going to share screen.

[00:36] (screen share starts)

[00:38] Sabrina James: So you’re seeing Redwood Console, this is a sandbox tenant. On the left nav we have a new entry point that says “Get to production” — wording may change, but for now it opens the checklist. The idea is: one place where you can see what’s done, what’s next, and deep link to the exact place in the Console or the exact doc.

[00:58] Ravi Singh: Is this like a guided tour thing or more like a list?

[01:02] Sabrina James: Mostly a list for MVP. Not the pop-up tour overlays. Each step has a status: Not started, In progress, Complete, and sometimes “Needs attention” if we detect like repeated 401s or a bunch of 429s. That last part is not fully automated yet, but we’re heading there.

[01:19] Jordan Ellis: What are the steps right now?

[01:21] Sabrina James: Let me open it. Okay, so first is “Create API key,” then “Make your first successful request,” then “Enable streaming,” “Set timeouts and retries,” “Review usage dashboard,” “Configure quotas/budgets,” “Pin a model version,” “Set fallback policy,” and “Add basic observability hooks.”

[01:43] Avery Park: That’s pretty close to what we’ve been doing manually.

[01:47] Sabrina James: Right, and we’re trying to make it explicit and consistent across languages and environments.

[01:53] Ben Carter: And on our side, it reduces those early support tickets like auth mistakes, rate limit surprises, and streaming disconnect confusion.

[02:00] Ravi Singh: Can I ask—how do you detect “complete”? Like, do you just assume if someone clicked the doc it’s done?

[02:07] Sabrina James: Good question. For a bunch of steps we compute completion based on server-side events. For example: “first successful request” becomes complete when we see a first 2xx response for that tenant. “Streaming enabled” becomes complete when we see a streaming session established—like an SSE connection that actually returns tokens.

[02:25] Ravi Singh: So you’re instrumenting gateway logs?

[02:27] Sabrina James: Essentially, yes. It’s emitted from the gateway/control plane side, not relying on the client to tell us. We do have light client hints sometimes, like user-agent tags, but the canonical signals are server-side.

[02:40] Avery Park: And privacy wise, you’re not sending prompts into this event stream, right?

[02:45] Sabrina James: Correct, no prompts. It’s like: event name, timestamp, tenant ID, maybe model ID, and request type. No raw content, no PII. Wei can go deeper on docs language later.

[02:57] Wei Chen: Yeah, the docs call out “no prompts, no completions” and the retention window. Also we flag what’s optional.

[03:06] Jordan Ellis: Can we see what the UI looks like when you click a step?

[03:10] Sabrina James: Yep. Clicking “Configure quotas/budgets” opens a drawer with: why it matters, what “good” looks like, and a big button that says “Go to Quotas.” And there’s a “Read guide” link which goes to the exact section in docs.

[03:25] Ravi Singh: The thing we hit with a different provider was: we thought we had a quota, but it was more like rate limit, and we still blew spend. So what does this mean in Redwood?

[03:35] Ben Carter: Yeah, let’s unpack that. In Redwood, rate limits are about request/token throughput. Quotas/budgets are about allowed usage over a period. Today we have quota limits and alerting, and we’re improving that UX.

[03:48] Avery Park: We’re specifically worried about, like, a runaway loop. If a job goes crazy at 2 AM, we want it to stop. Not just email us.

[03:58] Sabrina James: Totally. Right now: you can set a quota ceiling that will reject requests once you exceed it—so it’s a “hard stop” at the API layer. Alerts are additional. The nuance is the lag between usage metering and enforcement, depending on where the request is handled.

[04:15] Ravi Singh: There’s always lag.

[04:16] Sabrina James: Yeah. For Hosted API, enforcement is close to real-time but not millisecond-perfect. Usually it’s within minutes, sometimes faster. But the usage dashboard can lag more because it’s aggregated.

[04:29] Jordan Ellis: That lag is what freaks product teams out. They see the dashboard and think nothing’s happening.

[04:33] Wei Chen: We added a callout in the new docs that says “usage dashboard updates within X minutes” and where to check raw request logs if you need immediate verification.

[04:43] Avery Park: What is X?

[04:44] Wei Chen: We’re currently saying “up to ~15 minutes” for the dashboard under normal load. It’s not a hard SLA, but we’re trying to be transparent.

[04:54] Ben Carter: And the checklist step “Review usage dashboard” will include that note so folks don’t think they misconfigured.

[05:01] Ravi Singh: Okay. Can we jump to the quickstart piece? I want to see the “production safe defaults” you mentioned in email.

[05:08] Sabrina James: Yep. So quickstart now starts with: set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var, run a minimal call, then we show streaming chat, and then we show how to add retries/timeouts. We also show structured logging. I’ll open the TypeScript version.

[05:25] (keyboard typing)

[05:28] Sabrina James: Alright. Here’s the snippet. Notice we default to a 60 second overall timeout and per-chunk timeout for streaming. Retries are enabled for retryable errors—like 429 and some 5xx—with exponential backoff and jitter.

[05:44] Ravi Singh: Are retries on by default? That can be dangerous.

[05:47] Sabrina James: In the SDK presets, you choose “production” vs “minimal.” Minimal is no retries. Production is recommended defaults. The checklist step “Set timeouts and retries” links to this and explains which errors are safe to retry and how to avoid duplicating side effects.

[06:05] Ravi Singh: What about idempotency keys?

[06:07] Sabrina James: For generate/chat, idempotency is supported at the request level. For tool calls that trigger side effects on your side, we advise: you must make your tool endpoint idempotent, because retries can call your tool again if you implement that pattern. The quickstart has a warning.

[06:24] Avery Park: That’s good. Our main workload is a chat widget in-app, but we also have a batch summarization job that can spike.

[06:32] Ben Carter: That’s helpful context. The checklist is geared toward both: first successful call, then streaming, then production guardrails.

[06:40] Jordan Ellis: For the checklist, do we have to do it in order? Like, we might not want streaming.

[06:45] Sabrina James: You don’t have to, but the UI is ordered and we recommend it. Steps can be skipped with a reason, but that’s more of an internal/admin feature today.

[06:56] Ravi Singh: You said “admin” — like support can mark steps done?

[06:59] Sabrina James: Yes, support can override in troubleshooting situations. For example, if we had an event ingestion issue and you definitely did the thing, support can mark it complete with an audit note.

[07:10] Avery Park: Does that mean you store all our onboarding events forever?

[07:14] Sabrina James: No. The onboarding events have a retention policy. The progress state is stored longer, but the raw event payloads rotate out. We can share the specifics; it’s aligned with our general telemetry retention.

[07:28] Ben Carter: We can send the data handling doc. It’s pretty explicit about what’s captured.

[07:33] Ravi Singh: Okay.

[07:35] Sabrina James: Let me actually show how completion looks. This tenant already has “API key created” complete. If I click “first successful request” it’s marked complete because we already ran calls. And then here’s “first streaming response”—it’s complete because we established streaming.

[07:54] Jordan Ellis: That’s nice. So the checklist is not just like “click checkboxes.”

[07:58] Sabrina James: Exactly.

[08:00] Ben Carter: Avery, can I ask: where are you currently? You said you’re using us in dev, right?

[08:06] Avery Park: Yeah, we have a proof-of-concept running. It’s basically one engineer using the Hosted API. We have not put it behind real user traffic. The big blocker is we don’t have confidence in spend controls and also we want a fallback if the model is slow.

[08:21] Sabrina James: Great. Those map directly to “quotas/budgets” and “fallback policy.” Let’s talk fallback: Redwood supports routing/fallback policies—like if the pinned model is at capacity or latency is above a threshold, we can fall back to a compatible variant.

[08:38] Ravi Singh: Like a smaller model?

[08:40] Sabrina James: Usually, yes. Or same family different quantization profile, depending. For MVP we’re keeping it simple: pick primary model, pick fallback model, define trigger conditions. The checklist step is “Set fallback policy,” and it deep links into the policy page.

[08:55] Jordan Ellis: But isn’t that a quality risk? Product doesn’t want weird responses.

[09:00] Sabrina James: It is a tradeoff. We recommend you run a small eval set comparing primary vs fallback and decide what’s acceptable. We can help with that.

[09:10] Ben Carter: Practically, it keeps you online. Especially at launch.

[09:14] Ravi Singh: Okay, back to cost controls. We want: (1) a monthly cap, (2) alerts at like 50%, 80%, 100%, and (3) maybe a per-day cap for batch jobs.

[09:28] Wei Chen: The docs quickstart now includes an example of alerting. There’s also Terraform snippets for budgets/alerts if you manage it as code.

[09:36] Ravi Singh: Does the API support setting that? Or only in UI.

[09:40] Sabrina James: Today primarily UI for Hosted, but we have APIs for some settings. If you’re Terraform-first we can point to what exists now and what’s coming.

[09:50] Avery Park: We also need to explain this internally. Like, we need to show our finance person, “Here is the plan and the guardrails.”

[09:58] Ben Carter: That’s actually why we’re building the “first production launch” checklist. It’s a communication artifact as much as it is product UX.

[10:06] Jordan Ellis: Can we export it? Like a PDF.

[10:09] Sabrina James: Not in MVP. But you can share a link to the checklist state. Export is on the roadmap.

[10:16] Ravi Singh: Another thing: we got 429s during a test. It wasn’t huge traffic. It confused us.

[10:23] Sabrina James: Right—so 429 can be either rate limit or quota enforcement. In our responses we include headers that indicate which one. The checklist step “Handle 429 and retries” will call that out, and the SDK presets implement backoff.

[10:38] Ravi Singh: We didn’t see those headers in our client.

[10:41] Sabrina James: It depends if your HTTP client is surfacing response headers. In the updated examples we log the request ID and the rate-limit headers. Also if you’re using the OpenAI compat layer, it can mask some headers depending on the library.

[10:55] Ravi Singh: We are using OpenAI compat. Our codebase is built around that.

[10:59] Ben Carter: That’s common. We can make sure you’re on the latest compat package; we added better user-agent tagging and some header passthrough improvements.

[11:08] Avery Park: Also we saw streaming disconnect once. Not sure if it was us.

[11:12] Sabrina James: Streaming disconnects happen. The important thing is a reconnect strategy. Our Go SDK has a reconnect helper now, and the TS example shows how to resume or degrade gracefully. The checklist step “Enable streaming” includes a sub-bullet: “implement reconnect / handle partial responses.”

[11:29] Jordan Ellis: What do you recommend from a UX perspective? If streaming drops, do we show an error or continue.

[11:34] Sabrina James: We typically recommend: show partial response, display “connection interrupted, retrying,” and attempt a retry if safe. For chat, sometimes you can retry the same prompt; for tool calls it’s trickier.

[11:49] Ravi Singh: Okay.

[11:51] Sabrina James: Let me show the checklist step details for “Observability hooks.” It includes: “capture request_id,” “log model and latency,” “emit client-side metrics,” and optionally enable tracing. We have a minimal snippet.

[12:06] Avery Park: Do we need to integrate OpenTelemetry to get value?

[12:09] Sabrina James: Not required. You can start with structured logs and a couple counters. If you do have OTel, we can hook in.

[12:18] Ben Carter: The big early win is: when something fails, you can send our support a request ID and we can find it.

[12:25] Ravi Singh: That’s good.

[12:27] Jordan Ellis: Can we talk about the “model pinning” step? We got nervous when we saw the model name we were using changed behavior.

[12:34] Sabrina James: Yep. By default you might be on “latest” for a model family. We recommend pinning to an exact version for production. The checklist step is literally “Pin a model version,” and it links to the model settings page.

[12:48] Avery Park: So we can keep dev on latest but prod pinned.

[12:52] Sabrina James: Exactly.

[12:54] Ravi Singh: And the fallback policy respects pinning too?

[12:57] Sabrina James: Yes. You choose specific versions.

[13:00] Ben Carter: This also helps with internal approvals: you can show “we’re on version X.”

[13:06] Avery Park: So, the objections I have are basically two: one is spend controls, the other is can we be confident this checklist is actually accurate. Like, if it says “done,” is it done.

[13:17] Sabrina James: On accuracy: because it’s server-side events, it’s pretty reliable. The one tricky thing we saw in dogfooding is event ordering—like events arriving out of order causing step regressions. We fixed that with monotonic transitions and idempotency keys.

[13:35] Ravi Singh: Okay, that’s reassuring. On spend: do you have examples of customers setting hard caps.

[13:41] Ben Carter: We do. It usually looks like: set a monthly quota, set alert thresholds, and in your app implement your own internal circuit breaker too. Like if you exceed your own metric, degrade features. We can share a pattern.

[13:56] Jordan Ellis: That’s the thing, we want the platform to enforce it, not our app.

[14:00] Sabrina James: Understood. Today we can enforce quota at the API layer, with the caveat on aggregation delay. If you want true per-minute spend stop, you usually still add a client side guard.

[14:13] Ravi Singh: Like limiting max tokens per request.

[14:15] Sabrina James: Exactly. That’s also in the checklist: “set max_output_tokens and timeouts.”

[14:23] Wei Chen: The quickstart now uses explicit max tokens. The old one didn’t.

[14:28] Avery Park: That helps.

[14:30] Ben Carter: Can I ask what your target timeline is for first production traffic?

[14:35] Avery Park: If we can get comfortable, two to three weeks. We want to test with internal users first, then a small cohort.

[14:43] Ben Carter: Great. Our suggested plan: we enable this checklist flag for your sandbox tenant so you can see it end-to-end, and Sabrina can do a follow-up specifically on quotas/budgets and the fallback policy.

[14:55] Ravi Singh: Can we get a copy of the checklist steps as text? I want to paste it into our internal doc.

[15:00] Wei Chen: Yes, we can send the canonical list. It’s also becoming a docs page.

[15:06] Jordan Ellis: And if we run into 401 issues, is that part of checklist too?

[15:10] Sabrina James: The first steps include API key creation and env var setup, and there’s troubleshooting. We added common mistakes: wrong key, whitespace, using a project key in org context, things like that.

[15:25] Avery Park: Nice.

[15:26] Ben Carter: Do you want to see anything else in the demo? Or should we spend the remaining time on Q&A.

[15:32] Ravi Singh: I’d like to understand how you attribute “first success.” Like if we call embeddings vs chat.

[15:38] Sabrina James: For now, “first success” is any 2xx on our core inference routes (chat/generate/embeddings). We might break it down later. The goal is to reduce time from signup to a working request.

[15:54] Ravi Singh: That makes sense. For our product, chat is the relevant one.

[15:58] Jordan Ellis: Are you going to nag users? Like, does it pop up every time.

[16:02] Sabrina James: Not right now. It’s visible but not intrusive. There’s a small banner on the overview page for new tenants, but you can dismiss.

[16:11] Avery Park: Okay, good.

[16:13] Ben Carter: Switching gears: you mentioned you tried other providers. Anything you liked or disliked that we should know?

[16:20] Avery Park: We used OpenAI early. It’s easy but expensive and not much control. We looked at Bedrock for enterprise reasons but it felt heavy. Together was okay but we had inconsistent latency.

[16:32] Ben Carter: Got it. Redwood’s angle is consistent serving plus more knobs, without making you build infra.

[16:38] Ravi Singh: We like knobs, but only if they’re safe. Like we don’t want to accidentally lower quality.

[16:43] Sabrina James: That’s why the checklist includes “pin model,” “fallback,” and “observability” as guardrails. And we’re trying to make the default settings safe.

[16:54] Jordan Ellis: One last question: can we set different quotas for different environments? Like staging vs prod.

[17:00] Sabrina James: Yes, per project/environment. Most teams create separate projects. The checklist encourages that: “Create separate keys for dev and prod.”

[17:10] Ravi Singh: Perfect.

[17:12] (small crosstalk)

[17:13] Avery Park: What do you need from us to turn on the sandbox feature flag.

[17:17] Ben Carter: Just confirm the tenant/org ID or the email domain you’re signing up with. We can do it quickly.

[17:24] Avery Park: We’ll send it.

[17:26] Sabrina James: And once it’s enabled, I’d love for you to click through and tell us what’s confusing. We’re still tuning copy and step order.

[17:36] Jordan Ellis: Yeah, I can do that.

[17:38] Ben Carter: Great. Let’s do a quick recap and next steps.

[17:42] Ben Carter: (recap) We showed the checklist in Console and the updated quickstart with streaming + production defaults. Your key concerns are: hard-ish spend caps, clarity on quotas vs rate limits, and usage dashboard lag. Next: we’ll enable the checklist in your sandbox tenant, send you links to the quickstart and the checklist steps, and schedule a follow-up focused on quotas/budgets and fallback policy.

[18:04] Avery Park: Sounds good.

[18:06] Ravi Singh: Yep.

[18:07] Jordan Ellis: Works.

[18:09] Ben Carter: Cool, I’ll email right after. Thanks all.

[18:12] (call continues with informal scheduling chatter; transcript truncated by recorder)

[18:20] Sabrina James: I’ll also send recommended retry settings for streaming, because that’s usually where things get weird.

[18:25] Avery Park: Great, thank you.

[18:27] Ben Carter: Alright, talk soon.
